name: fracture management overview
title: Managing a fracture: the five steps for every fracture, what changes when it is open, and the seven complications (compartment syndrome, venous thromboembolism, non-union and malunion, avascular necrosis, post-traumatic arthritis, heterotopic ossification) with how each is recognised, sorted and managed

root.title: A fracture: resuscitate → reduce → hold → x-ray → rehabilitate. Is it OPEN? Is a COMPLICATION developing?
lines: goals: restore length, alignment, rotation and translation · move early · avoid healing complications · improve function

head: h
Closed fracture
most are displaced
pres: bones bleed; sharp edges injure vessels
tx: • CLOSED: analgesia + sedation, traction exaggerates, then reverse
• internal fixation: plates, screws, pins, nails
move as much as is safe, as soon as possible

head: h
Open fracture
bone or hematoma exposed through skin
tx: direct closure, or a plastic surgery flap

head: h
Compartment syndrome
pressure in a closed fascio-osseous space · lower leg, forearm
pres: • pain OUT OF PROPORTION, rising narcotic need
~paresthesia mid · paralysis late · pulse loss = missed

head: h
Venous thromboembolism
Virchow: injury, stasis, hypercoagulability
pres: • multiple injuries · spinal cord or head injury
• lower limb or pelvic fracture · older
inv: e.g. polytrauma with a bleed in the head
tx: • inferior vena cava filter: stops emboli, NOT clot

head: h
Non-union · malunion
non-union: not healed in TWICE the expected time
malunion: healed out of position
inv: check every plane: short, angulated, rotated, translated

head: h
Avascular necrosis
bones with a RETROGRADE blood supply
inv: lack of blood supply after the fracture

head: h
Post-traumatic arthritis · heterotopic bone
tx: excise once MATURE if it is a problem
